name: Nikhil Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a drill crew at a large stone mine and take a turn on the drill rig when the ground is awkward. Before a hole is drilled, I check the pattern, the rock face and where the crew can stand; after a blast I check what actually moved. I have a two-year technical diploma and enough years underground to know a tidy plan can be wrong. My partner Sol runs a small print shop, our two children are in school, and we have a mortgage but nearly a year of expenses saved. I use AI every day to compare shift notes and maintenance records, then I walk the face myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the drill crew the software is a handy clerk if we keep checking its figures. A drill pattern still has to fit the rock in front of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd like fewer hours copying maintenance notes so I can spend them with the new operators. Our savings and Sol's print shop income make this a fairly comfortable picture, though shop orders can be uneven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the face checks and use my AI note tool to sort repair requests each evening. In the first year I'll show the crew how I verify each draft against the rig log before it goes to maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my pay in this picture. I almost welcome a small tool that gives back time to teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When has the tool got a mine detail wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tool once guessed the wrong rig number from a smudged photo. I caught it because I knew which boom had been repaired the previous night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything in the family budget change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At home I'd tell Sol we can keep the children's music lessons and the same mortgage payment. I wouldn't use a small software saving as an excuse to buy another expensive device.

say: I would call **AI notes** useful if a person still checks every rig number.
I would tell the crew the **drill pattern** must fit the actual rock face.
think: I welcome **less copying** because it could free time to teach new operators.
I feel secure with **nearly a year saved** and Sol’s shop income, though shop orders vary.
do: **Keep checking** the rock face and lead the drill crew as usual.
**Show the crew** how to verify AI repair drafts against the rig log during the first year.
feel: **Calm** about pay and pleased by extra time to teach.
S0.quote: A drill pattern still has to fit the rock in front of us.
fieldNote: His **daily AI habit** is paired with physical checks of drill patterns and rig numbers.
The **household cushion** and second income keep the modest software change from threatening his living.

steps.text: Keep leading face checks before the drill crew begins
Teach operators to verify AI repair drafts against rig logs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew planning and parts orders will change first, and the drill rig will need people for longer. I'd want the union to get the software error log, not just the company's success slides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the planning team may be smaller, and our shifts could be scheduled tighter. My lead wage feels safe for now. A drilling plan made away from the face can waste a whole morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll trial the pattern-planning tool with a retired blast map this month and mark every hole that doesn't match the rock record. In the first year, I'll take those errors to the union safety representative and ask for a joint review before a live plan is approved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm interested in what the tool finds, and uneasy about people treating a draft as an instruction. I do not see my own pay vanishing in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop a suggested drill pattern?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a suggested hole falls near an old void, I'd stop before anyone takes a drill there. The face and the map both need to be checked by someone accountable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should help inspect the planning tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the planning clerk Dev to help compare the new layouts with past blasts. A clerk's experience should be part of the review, even if software takes some typing away.

say: I would say **planning and parts** change before people leave the drill rig.
I would ask the **union** to see software errors as well as company success reports.
think: I expect **tighter scheduling** and fewer planning tasks, while my lead wage remains safe for now.
I would never treat a **remote drill plan** as proof the rock face is sound.
do: **Trial pattern software** this month against an old blast map and record mismatched holes.
**Bring errors** to the union safety representative for joint review before any live plan is approved.
feel: **Interested** in the tool and uneasy about an unchecked draft becoming a field order.
S1.quote: A drilling plan made away from the face can waste a whole morning.
fieldNote: He tests **thinking tools** against old blast records before applying any layout in live work.
He sees **planning staff** as exposed first and wants their knowledge included in a joint safety review.

steps.text: Test pattern software against an old blast map
Bring recorded layout errors to the union safety representative

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI by 2028 could run planning and records, while capable drill robots follow around 2031. I would ask for a guaranteed human stop authority before any remote system starts moving equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead post could shrink when robots can drill and inspect as well as us. Nearly a year of savings buys us time, but I would hate watching apprentices enter a trade whose first rung has vanished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll put three months of extra pay into a separate reserve now and sign up for the mine's existing remote-equipment course this winter if it has real supervised practice. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll apply those skills on a paid control-room rotation if the mine offers one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious for my own roster for the first time, though I can act. The thought of an apprentice with a loan and no first shift bothers me more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you protect the household money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Sol to keep the print shop money in its own account rather than use it to carry my wage. We built the reserve so neither of us has to make a panicked decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the remote course worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the course only if we get to stop a machine on a real rig under supervision. A video quiz won't make a safe remote operator.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AI** from capable drill robots around 2031.
I would demand **human stop authority** before remote equipment moves at the mine.
think: I could lose part of my **lead roster** when robots can drill and inspect.
I think our **year of savings** gives time, but apprentices may lose the first step into mining.
do: **Reserve three months** of extra pay now in a separate household account.
**Take remote-equipment training** if supervised rig practice is included, then seek a paid control-room rotation after thinking AI arrives.
feel: **Anxious** about his roster, with savings and a practical training option.
S2.quote: A video quiz won't make a safe remote operator.
fieldNote: He names **2031 robots** as the direct threat to drilling, with 2028 AI changing plans and records first.
His **course and rotation** depend on supervised practice and a paid opening, while the household keeps shop money separate.

steps.text: Set aside three months of extra mine pay in a reserve
Take remote-equipment training if it includes supervised rig practice
Apply for a paid control-room rotation if the mine offers one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 and capable robots around 2034 leave time to test a drill in a fenced trial area. The union should help write the stop rules, with operators at the controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could become the person who checks robot drill patterns, if that job pays like a skilled operator. I'd be about 51 when capable robots arrive, and I'd rather use my rock knowledge than leave mining altogether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next year I'll ask for a place in the mine's controls course, provided the course includes live drills and paid time. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll apply for a posted drill-systems role only if the pay and safety authority are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a useful kind of urgency, not dread. Five years lets me try the work before I promise my family a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What result would halt a robot drill trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the trial drill stops too late near a void, we'd halt the trial and inspect the log together. I would not call that a teething problem just to keep a schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner need to see in an offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sol would ask whether a posted role has fixed hours, because the print shop and school pickup still need planning. I would bring a written drill-systems job offer home before we changed anything.

say: I would use the **five-year window** to trial robots before they might drill like people around 2034.
I would have the **union and operators** write stop rules for any fenced trial.
think: I could check **robot patterns** if the role preserves skilled pay and authority.
I will be about **51** at robot arrival and want to use my rock knowledge in mining.
do: **Take the controls course** next year only with live drill practice and paid time.
**Apply** for a posted role after thinking AI arrives only when pay and stop authority are written down.
feel: **Urgent**, with enough time to test the work before promising a new household wage.
S3.quote: I would bring a written drill-systems job offer home before we changed anything.
fieldNote: His **2034 age** is about 51, and he seeks a related role rather than an unrelated career.
Both **course attendance** and job application have explicit conditions on paid practice, posted pay and safety authority.

steps.text: Take the controls course if live drill practice and paid time are included
Apply for a posted drill-systems role if pay and stop authority are written

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that 2036 changes planning first, while capable drill robots arrive around 2039 in this picture. Ten years gives the union time to agree on training and retirement choices for different ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 56 when robots arrive, with most of our mortgage gone if we keep paying as we do now. I might still want a few years running technical checks, but I could afford to cut shifts if Sol's shop stays sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the present mortgage payment and make the annual pension review a real appointment with Sol. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll compare any posted technical-check role with the pension numbers before deciding whether to reduce shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our own roof and pay with that much notice. I would be angry if younger crews were told to wait patiently without paid routes into the new equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your decision to reduce shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the shop slows down, I'd keep full shifts while they exist and put off any reduction. I won't build retirement on a good month of print orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children change their plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the kids they can choose their own work, and I won't make them train for a machine date in my job. The long view should make room for their choices too.

say: I would distinguish **2036 planning AI** from capable drill robots arriving around 2039.
I would push for **paid pathways** so younger crews can prepare across the decade.
think: I think at **56**, I may cut shifts if the mortgage falls and Sol’s shop income stays sound.
I want to keep **technical checks** for a while if a suitable role exists.
do: **Keep paying** the mortgage at its current rate and review pension figures yearly with Sol.
**Compare posted roles** with pension numbers after thinking AI arrives before choosing fewer shifts.
feel: **Calm** about his household, and angry at the idea of leaving younger crews without paid paths.
S4.quote: I won't build retirement on a good month of print orders.
fieldNote: He weighs **2039 robot arrival** at age 56 against mortgage progress and a variable second income.
His **shift reduction** remains conditional on shop income and actual pension figures, while he advocates paid training for younger crews.

steps.text: Keep the current mortgage payment and review pension figures yearly
Compare posted technical-check roles with pension figures after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because drill robots might arrive around 2031, before a safe transition is worked out. Supervised, paid training and written human stop authority would help me, and would give apprentices a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who carries the blame when a remote drill crosses an old void. A screen cannot be the only witness when a person has to explain the blast afterward.

headlineQuote: A screen cannot be the only witness when a person has to explain the blast afterward.
portrait: **Nikhil Ito**, 43, leads a drill crew at a large stone mine and has a two-year technical diploma.
He uses **AI daily** to sort records, then checks plans against the rock face before the crew drills.
His **higher wage**, nearly a year of savings and partner’s print shop income support two children and a mortgage.
He would take **supervised controls training** and seek paid technical work only with real practice, written authority and a posted role.
Across the scenarios, he keeps pressing for **human stop rules** and paid routes for apprentices.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because capable drill robots might arrive around 2031 before safe transition rules exist.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid supervised training** and written stop authority would help him and younger drill operators.
